claims.text: HEA coating wear resistance is primarily governed by the fraction and stability of ultra-fine grains.
Ultra-fine grains dynamically evolve into a protective nanocrystalline tribolayer during sliding.
The fine-grained microstructure limits plastic deformation and crack initiation.
Limiting plastic deformation and crack initiation reduces the wear rate.
The initial coating contains coarse grains and a minor fraction of ultra-fine grains.
A heat treatment or similar processing variation can increase the volume fraction and stability of ultra-fine grains without changing overall alloy chemistry.
Oxidation effects are minimal in the proposed room-temperature to below-600 °C abrasive-wear regime.
The dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer originates from the controlled ultra-fine grain fraction.
A higher fraction of stable ultra-fine grains facilitates adaptive grain-boundary processes, including dislocation blocking and local recrystallization.
These grain-boundary processes produce a continuous protective tribolayer.
The protective tribolayer minimizes plastic flow and delays crack initiation.
Increasing ultra-fine grain content will lower wear rates by potentially one to two orders of magnitude relative to the baseline.
The treated coating will exhibit smoother wear tracks and less debris because of enhanced protective-layer formation.
The proposed mechanism should apply primarily during abrasive wear below about 600 °C when tribo-oxidation and chemically reactive environments do not dominate.
